entries.title: Munich up against at least six competitors for 2036 Olympics
entries.summary: The International Olympic Committee has revealed the six other countries intending to bid for the 2036 Olympic Games. This comes after Germany selected Munich as its Olympic candidate.
entries.content:
October 6, 2026

The International Olympic Committee has revealed the six other countries intending to bid for the 2036 Olympic Games. This comes after Germany selected Munich as its Olympic candidate.

Munich's bid for the 2036 Summer Olympics will be up against at least six candidates from Europe, Asia and Africa. On Tuesday, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced that, in addition to Germany, Hungary, Turkey, India, Qatar, South Korea and South Africa all intend to bid for the Games. All are currently engaged in the Continuous Dialogue stage of the bidding process with the IOC.

However, there could be further applicants, as the deadline for interested parties to submit a bid is October 31. The candidates are to present their plans virtually to the Future Host Commission in November. In March 2027, the IOC is to deliberate, analyze, and narrow down the field of applicants to a group selected to enter into the Strategic Dialogue stage.

A subsequent Targeted Dialogue stage with one or more bidders is planned for 2028, with the final decision on the 2036 Olympic host expected at the IOC Session in the summer of 2029.

However, the IOC did not disclose exactly which cities, alongside Munich, are in the running – although Ahmedabad, Doha, Budapest and Istanbul are seen as possible hopefuls.

Munich secured its bid late last month after beating the Cologne/Rhine-Ruhr region in a vote by delegates of the German Olympic Sports Confederation. The city last hosted the Games in 1972. Berlin had withdrawn its bid in the days leading up to the vote.

'Best possible experience for the athletes'

"Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: Athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do," IOC President Kirsty Coventry said.

"As an athlete, you spend years working to make your Olympic dream come true. The experience you have when you finally reach the Olympic Games stays with you for the rest of your life," added the former swimmer who won gold in the 200-meter backstroke for Zimbabwe at the 2004 Athens and 2008 Beijing Summer Games.

"That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point."

Munich bid sees itself as well-positioned

The IOC is to evaluate the bidders' proposals based on "technical factors." These include a master plan for competition venues and the athlete experience, the financing strategy, political and public support, the capacity to deliver the event, and a sustainability strategy. The German Olympic Sports Confederation believes Munich is well-positioned in all these areas.

The Munich bid is not focused solely on 2036 but was also designed with 2040 and 2044 in mind. If it misses out on 2036, Munich can expect to face a similarly large pool of competitors for the following two Summer Games. According to an IOC statement, there are National Olympic Committees "taking part in noncommittal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036."

This article was adapted from German.

entries.title: French AI company announces new, private model
entries.summary: The company's new model, named "Le Chonk," is its first release in five months. Mistral says it outruns some of its Chinese competitors in several areas.
entries.content:
October 6, 2026

The company's new model, named "Le Chonk," is its first release in five months. Mistral says it outruns some of its Chinese competitors in several areas.

Frenchtech company Mistral on Tuesday announced the upcoming release of "Le Chonk," its biggest AIopen-weight model, aimed at users wanting to keep their data private.

Popular AI models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAIrely on closed models.

Le Chonk, officially named Mistral Large 4, will be made publicly available on October 27, with cybersecurity experts and government authorities receiving access to a version of the model with fewer safety restrictions to test its capabilities.

Last month, Mistral raised €3 billion euros ($3.4 billion), Europe's biggest technology fundraising.

The new AI model allows users to download and customize "weights" that determine how it computes on their own servers.

An open-weight model means a user can download the software and run it on their own hardware. While the top US models run on their own models, many of their Chinesecompetitors are open-weight.

Europe's AI hope

Mistral, considered Europe's leading AI company, said the new model outperforms many rival open-weight models.

Le Chonk is the three-year-old company's first new model release since May.

According to Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch, the new model is "actually above the Chinese models" in certain areas, including cyber.

"The narrative that Europe cannot compete is something that is not true," Mensch said at the company's event in Abu Dhabi, without specifying which Chinese models he was referring to.

MIstral has positioned itself as a safer European alternative in comparison to its main US competitors, especially given the latter companies' recent warnings regarding AI's dangers.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Naked Trump statue goes on display in Strasbourg
entries.summary: Titled "The Orange Plague," a gold-coated statue presents Donald Trump sitting on a smaller man's back. The Danish artist blamed Trump for getting in the way of efforts to address climate change.
entries.content:
United States of America

Naked Trump statue goes on display in Strasbourg

October 6, 2026

Titled "The Orange Plague," a gold-coated statue presents Donald Trump sitting on a smaller man's back. The Danish artist blamed Trump for getting in the way of efforts to address climate change.

A statue of US President Donald Trump was put on exhibit in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, France.

The 2.5-meter satirical statue, by Danish artist Jens Galschiot, is called "Orange Plague," and it shows the US leader naked, holding a long gold club and sitting on the shoulders of a smaller man.

The artist said it is coated with 23-karat gold. The statue is also known by the name "King of Injustice."

Next to the statue are cards explaining that the "King of Injustice" is "sitting on the back of a man" who is sinking under the burden.

"I would do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back," the card continues, with the artist blaming Trump for hindering attempts to confront climate change.

No comment from Trump

The statue stands at an intersection connecting two of the parliament's buildings, and is scheduled to remain there until Thursday.

Left-wing Danish European Parliament member Per Clausen, who invited the artist, said he is not worried about a potential reaction by Trump.

"If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage," Clausen said.

The US president has not commented on the statue, which has also been on display in other European cities as well as at the COP30 UN climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

entries.title: Germany shaken by espionage and treason allegations
entries.summary: The former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, has been accused of spying for a foreign country. Never before has a German official of August Hanning's stature been accused of treason.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany shaken by espionage and treason allegations

October 6, 2026

The former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, has been accused of spying for a foreign country. Never before has a German official of August Hanning's stature been accused of treason.

If the allegations are confirmed, it would be an espionage case of historic proportions for Germany: August Hanning, former head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), has been arrested, with the federal prosecutor accusing him of espionage, treason and attempted treason.

August Hanning, now 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. But even before then, he had enjoyed a meteoric rise within the security apparatus. After leaving the BND, he served as state secretary in the Federal Interior Ministry, then moved into the private sector and worked as a security consultant.

According to the federal prosecutor's office, his informant was his former chief-of-staff, named in the statement only as Manfred D.*, who went on to hold this position under Hanning's successors from March 2012 to March 2026. D. thus had access to a great deal of classified information.

Classified information from the chancellor's office

Manfred D. is alleged to have passed on nearly 2,000 BND documents — some of them highly sensitive — to Hanning over the course of several years in exchange for money. Hanning is then said to have used the information in his private consultancy business.

The most serious allegation is that Hanning is said to have maintained close contact with an employee of a foreign intelligence service for years and to have leaked classified information to him. It is not known which country was involved, but reports say it is not Russia.

Investigators also mention an analysis that Hanning is said to have prepared for an employee of another foreign intelligence service. However, it is not certain whether the analysis ever reached that person.

The classified information also concerned the routine meetings of the heads of German security agencies at the chancellery. Topics included, among other things, the Iranian nuclear program and analyses of the Russian armed forces.

Since intelligence from foreign partner agencies is also said to have been shared in this context, this could also undermine their trust in the German BND and lead to difficulties in future intelligence cooperation with Germany.

Hanning came under scrutiny in an entirely different context

"A good agent is one who doesn't draw attention to himself," Hanning was once quoted as saying. When he finally drew attention to himself, it was in an entirely different context.

In September 2025, the Hamburg state police searched Hanning's home and offices in connection with the famous case of the kidnapping involving Christina Block, heiress to the steakhouse restaurant chain Block House. State prosecutors in Hamburg accused her of having ordered the kidnapping of her two youngest children in late 2023 due to a custody dispute.

A little over a year before the operation to bring the children back, there is said to have already been a failed kidnapping attempt. At the time, there were suspicions that Hanning was involved, which he denies.

But during a search in 2025, investigators found an electronic storage device containing top-secret BND documents. The police handed the documents over to the federal prosecutor's office, which launched a covert investigation against Hanning and Manfred D. in May 2026. The most recent documents found so far are said to date from June 2022.

Greens demand consequences

Throughout its history, the BND has seen a number of espionage cases, some of them spectacular. In the 1960s, Heinz Felfe headed the "Counterintelligence: Soviet Union" division while simultaneously working for the Soviet secret service, the KGB.

In 2014, a BND employee was exposed as a spy for the US CIA. There is also an ongoing trial against a BND agent accused of betraying secrets to Russia's FSB in September and October 2022 — that is, after the start of the war in Ukraine. Yet never before has a former official of August Hanning's stature been at the center of suspicion of espionage.

"The BND launched extensive internal investigations early on and without delay, which corroborated the suspicions," said current BND President Martin Jäger. "For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security."

However, there was some fierce criticism from the political sphere. Günter Krings of the conservative governing party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told the Rheinische Post newspaper: "The mere suspicion that a former BND chief is selling secrets is damaging to trust in our security agencies."

Konstantin von Notz of the environmentalist Green Party and deputy chair of the parliamentary committee that oversees the intelligence services said: "These are serious and grave allegations that have been leveled against August Hanning." Speaking on behalf of his party, he called for greater scrutiny of lobbying activities by former top officials and those with the highest security clearances. "These are clearly also a gateway for hostile intelligence services," von Notz said. The federal government must put an immediate stop to these "illegitimate practices."

Clara Bünger, domestic policy spokesperson for the socialist Left Party group in the Bundestag, went even further: "The investigations against former BND chief Hanning show once again: The intelligence services themselves are a security risk."

This article was originally written in German.

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

entries.title: EU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members
entries.summary: The European Commission has put forward ideas it hopes will both ease the EU expansion process and allay concerns among existing members. Several countries, not least war-torn Ukraine, are among the candidates.
entries.content:
Europe

EU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members

October 6, 2026

The European Commission has put forward ideas it hopes will both ease the EU expansion process and allay concerns among existing members. Several countries, not least war-torn Ukraine, are among the candidates.

The European Commission on Tuesday published a document called "Preparing for a wider Union," which sought to lay out new proposals on "the policy orientations and actions needed to prepare the [European] Union for future enlargements." 

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europe's future depends on the choices we make today," as she tries to encourage progress at the EU's leaders' summit this month and in other upcoming talks on the matter. 

The EU's executive proposed an array of changes — including a gradual integration process for would-be members, new safeguards "to ensure that commitments undertaken during accession negotiations continue to be fulfiled steadily after accession," and changes to voting rules.

They were trying to strike a balance between simplifying the accession process, incentivizing candidate countries to continue to pursue it, and allaying concerns among existing members about potential risks or costs of expansion.

Why is expansion coming back into focus?

In the quarter century after the end of the Cold War, the EU rapidly grew from a union of 12 member states to 28, before dipping back down to 27 when the UK left following 2016's Brexit referendum. 

But the process has ground to a halt ever since, with a series of candidate countries stuck in lengthy negotiations and little apparent appetite among members to continue to expand.

In recent years, amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine and signs of the US vying for increased influence in parts of Europe, theoretical interest in expansion has picked up once more. But realizing the idea, with strict rules governing the accession process and the need for unanimous support among existing members for many core steps, has remained challenging. 

What did the Commission say about expansion?

Von der Leyen said the Commission was trying to prepare institutions, adapt policies and adjust budgets to reflect shared realities to better facilitate and accommodate expansion.

"Enlargement of our Union is a geopolitical imperative," she said. "Today, we are laying the groundwork to ensure that a larger Union is also a stronger one: more resilient, more effective, and firmly anchored in the values and rules that define us."

She said that as countries progress on their path towards reform, "the EU must be ready to welcome them."

Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that Brussels' assessment "shows that the EU can accommodate a larger membership." But "there are areas where we see challenges we need to address," she acknowledged.

"One is the rule of law and sincere cooperation, where we are proposing stronger possibilities to prevent backsliding, including reducing funding or restricting voting rights," Kos said.

What changes are the European Commission proposing?

The Commission lays out a number of proposed changes or policies designed to smooth the accession process, including but not limited to:

  • Moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting among members in a number of the less significant votes about advancing or progressing membership bids
  • It makes no mention of changing the current requirement for a unanimous vote about finalizing membership applications, however
  • Gradual and accelerated integration of candidate countries to "bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses," but which would remain "conditional and reversible"
  • "Stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitements undertaken during the acession negotiations" in future accession treaties, which could "in the most serious cases" extend to the suspension of voting rights
  • Introducing "targeted arrangements" to "significantly limit financial support and market access" for sensitive agricultural products from candidate country Ukraine
  • Ukraine's vast agricultural sector had prompted some concerns among EU members looking at how the bloc's budget could handle expansion, given that agriculture is a rare policy area where the bulk of spending and subsidies are orchestrated at the EU level, not by national governments

All these proposals will be subject to further discussion among European leaders and governments, with the next major meeting being next week's EU leaders' summit. Should they gain traction and progress, no doubt after some alterations and amendments along the way, they would ultimately have to face and pass various voting procedures to be implemented.

What's the current situation with EU candidate countries?

A total of eight countries currently have formal candidate status, meaning they are seeking to join the EU and have at least begun the often lengthy process that involves.

Some hope to join the bloc sooner rather than later, not least frontrunner Montenegro, after years of negotiations. Kos told DW last week that Montenegro was currently on track to become the next EU member by 2028. 

Others, like Turkey, have nominally been candidates for decades but have made no discernible progress for years.

Ukraine is the newest addition to the list, having only gained full candidate status in 2024, but it is also the one with the most pressing motivation to hurry the process along amid Russia's invasion.

Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, North Macedonia and Serbia are also all seeking membership.

A ninth country, Kosovo, is recognized as a potential candidate but not a formal one — with not all EU members recognizing Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia. 

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Russia denies anti-plague measures after pneumonia death
entries.summary: The death of an employee at an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk is still being looked into, the authorities said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for Russia to be transparent about its findings.
entries.content:
October 6, 2026

The death of an employee at an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk is still being looked into, the authorities said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for Russia to be transparent about its findings.

Russiadenied claims that it was imposing anti-plague measures following the death of a laboratory technician of pneumonic plague.

The woman worked at the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region.

The authorities in Russia, however, said the cause of death is yet to be confirmed, and Moscow's health authority Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims the country had put special measures in place.

Authorities deny reports of plague

According to Rospotrebnadzor, the information "does not originate from official sources" and is "untrue," with Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev adding that the inspection had found that the woman's death was a result of pneumonia.

"No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said.

Plague is a disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, known to be the most contagious and potentially fatal if not treated early.

Some reports in Russia suggested the woman could have caught the disease from a broken test tube, while others speculated on a potential link between her death and a lab accident at the institute.

The woman may have come into contact with up to 200 people, all of whom are under quarantine, according to one report.

World Health Organization monitoring situation

The World Health Organization (WHO) said the information it had received from Russia suggests that "no case" of the disease has so far been recorded in Irkutsk. 

Russia has launched an epidemiological investigation into a case of pneumonia, labeled as "community acquired," in an employee at the Irkutsk Institute.

"Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens" in the people who came into contact with the person, the WHO said, adding that the agency estimates the risk to be "moderate to low" for Irkutsk.

The WHO is still monitoring the situation closely, it said.

US President Donald Trump said he will discuss the case with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump also said the US intelligence is in "very deep discussions" on the matter, while also calling the disease "rough."

"That's a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” the US president told reporters at the White House.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is monitoring the situation.

According to Rubio, Russia needs to "share more information with the world."

Editor: Sean Sinico

entries.title: France’s conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests
entries.summary: Prime Minister Lecornu is pledging to improve schools at a time when the government seeks to save billions. France's dilemma can be seen across the EU: How to cut spending when citizens are demanding more from the state?
entries.content:
France

France's conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests

October 6, 2026

Prime Minister Lecornu is pledging to improve schools at a time when the government seeks to save billions. France's dilemma can be seen across the EU: How to cut spending when citizens are demanding more from the state?

France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is unlikely to have had a quiet weekend. For almost two weeks, students across France have been protesting, angered by class cancellations, overcrowded classrooms and run-down school buildings. The protests have increasingly been overshadowed by serious clashes with police.

At the same time, the government accuses the left-wing party La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting the protests for political purposes and fueling the blockades.

On Friday, Education Minister Edouard Geffray tried to ease tensions by meeting with student representatives. It was unsuccessful.

Instead, a nationwide day of protest took place on Tuesday.

On Sunday evening, the prime minister took charge of the crisis. In a letter to several ministers, Lecornu called for concrete proposals: Class cancellations should be addressed more quickly, school buildings should be upgraded to cope with hotter summers, and the controversial university admissions system "Parcoursup" should become more transparent.

Initial decisions, along with funding and a timetable, are expected to be announced this month. But Macron's ally Lecornu faces one key problem: He has to promise young people more government support while his government is imposing an austerity budget on the entire country.

A signal to the markets

Last Thursday, the government submitted its 2027 budget proposal to parliament. The budget deficit is expected to fall from a projected 5.4 % of economic output this year to 5% in 2027. To make up the shortfall, the government plans to make spending cuts worth billions of euros. France is already subject to an EU excessive deficit procedure and is expected to bring its budget gap back toward the 3% limit set by the European Union.

"It is an austerity budget," says Eileen Keller of the Franco-German Institute (dfi) in Ludwigsburg. At the same time, the draft is a signal to the financial markets. The government wants to show "that it is taking responsibility" and lay out a path toward reducing the deficit.

No majority in sight for the budget

The government plans to cut spending by the state itself, local and regional authorities, as well as in the social sector. Overall, Paris aims to reduce the budget by around €54 billion ($60.8 billion) compared with previously projected spending plans. Pensions alone are expected to make savings to the tune of around €5.5 billion, and more cuts are also planned in healthcare.

Whether the budget will actually be passed in its current form is still wide open. Lecornu's government does not have a parliamentary majority and relies on opposition votes. But with presidential elections coming next spring, an austerity budget is even less attractive to the opposition than it would otherwise be.

More money for schools — and more protests

The issue of education in particular shows that France's problem cannot be reduced to the formula "The state is cutting too much." The education budget is set to increase by around €1.2 billion in 2027. At the same time, the government expects around 1.7 million fewer schoolchildren by 2035.

For Keller, this contradiction shows that money is only part of the problem. Public dissatisfaction is linked to what she calls "priorities" and the fundamental direction of the education system, including the transition from school to higher education.

Financing education is getting more costly

The difficult outlook for France is compounded by another factor: the financial markets. For many years, France was used to financing its high levels of debt at relatively low interest rates. But those days are over. The yield on 10-year French government bonds has risen sharply in recent weeks. At times, the spread over German government bonds widened to around 1.5 percentage points, the highest level since the euro debt crisis in the 2010s. The business daily Les Echos ran the headline on Monday that the country was in the "eye of the cyclone."

Market skepticism is hitting France at a particularly difficult time. With debt at around 119% of economic output, France is almost twice as heavily indebted as Germany, whose debt ratio stands at around 64%.

Step by step, old government bonds that were issued at very low interest rates are increasingly having to be replaced with new and more expensive debt. The effects of this are clearly visible in the 2027 budget. Estimated around €74 billion, the government will have to spend more on its interest payments than it can afford to spend on schools or defense. According to Finance Minister Roland Lescure, interest payments already consume more than half of the overall budget deficit.

Keller stresses that it is therefore crucial that France continues to be seen by investors as a "credible debtor." These days, however, that credibility depends on more than just economic data.

Markets keeping a close eye on election campaigns

In spring 2027, the French will elect a new president. "The election campaign, which is now gaining intensity, is being watched by the financial markets," Keller says. In an analysis for the dfi, she puts the need for fiscal consolidation at between €75 billion and €160 billion, depending on the calculation.

From the markets' perspective, political consensus on the need for the nation to tighten its belt would be helpful. But, at present, there is no sign of clarity. How the burden will be shared in the future is instead likely to become a central issue in the election campaign.

A French problem with a European dimension

France is an especially acute case. But many other European countries are also currently grappling with fiscal consolidation and how to finance the state. Europe wants to spend more on defense, modernizing its infrastructure and transitioning to renewable energy sources. At the same time, citizens still expect a certain standard of education, pensions and healthcare.

In France, this conflict can be observed almost in real time. The issue is not only whether the government can respond to the demands of young people, but also whether it can avoid further violence. In Paris, many are wary of the prospect of a new broad-based social movement, like the Yellow Vests protests of the past. For Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, the coming days will be a major test.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: UK: Seventh arrest made after air base plot
entries.summary: The man, a British national in his twenties, was arrested in London in suspicion of "preparing terrorist acts."
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK: Seventh arrest made after air base plot

October 6, 2026

The man, a British national in his twenties, was arrested in London in suspicion of "preparing terrorist acts."

Police in the UK arrested a man in connection with an alleged planned attack on a military air base used by the United States.

The suspect, a 22-year-old British national, was arrested "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts," police said.

Police arrested the man in London, and he is the seventh person taken into custody in connection with the incident in which three vans were stopped near the RAF Fairford air base in England's southwest on September 27.

While no explosives were found in the van, police secured some gasoline in them, it said.

The other six suspects were also men in their 20s, including one who is a dual UK-Iranian national. All six have been released on bail.

Media reports in the UK said one of the initial suspects had informed the authorities of the incident, which police did not confirm.

Bombers withdrawn

US bombers have been seen taking off and landing at the air base, with the UK government allowing Washington to use it for "specific defensive operations into Iran."

US President Donald Trump said Washington had withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford due to "threats" possibly linked to Iran. At the same time, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down specific threats.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said there were "strong indications" that Iranhad a role in the incident, with British authorities labeling it "major." The UK also insists the RAF Fairford air base is safe.

Tehran rejected any involvement.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Paramount and Warner Bros merge into one Hollywood giant
entries.summary: Paramount has completed an $81 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as its owner Skydance creates a new entertainment behemoth. Billionaire David Ellison's hostile takeover bid defeated rival efforts from Netflix.
entries.content:
October 6, 2026

Paramount has completed an $81 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as its owner Skydance creates a new entertainment behemoth. Billionaire David Ellison's hostile takeover bid defeated rival efforts from Netflix.

Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles. 

The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal.

The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation. 

Why Skydance Corp.? Who's behind the new behemoth?

The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros.

The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through. 

"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump.

Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.

The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.

As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max.

Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. Former Mattel boss Ynon Kreiz is operating as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations.

Skydance Corp. looks set to have a total revenue in the region of $70 billion, based on the performance to date of its component parts. It says it's targeting cost savings of around $6 billion within three years as it takes advantage of overlaps created by the merger.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Spain court lifts Puigdemont arrest warrant, clearing way for his return home ahead of November elections
entries.summary: Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont fled Spain in 2017 after launching an independence bid. The court's decision means he can return home without fear of arrest after almost a decade in exile.
entries.content:
Spain

Catalan separatist Puigdemont cleared to return to Spain

October 6, 2026

Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont fled Spain in 2017 after launching an independence bid. The court's decision means he can return home without fear of arrest after almost a decade in exile.

Spain's Supreme Court on Tuesday lifted an arrest warrant for Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont, paving the way for him to return home ahead of a general election next month.

Puigdemont fled to Belgium in 2017 after leading a failed attempt for the wealthy northeastern Catalonia region to break away from Spain.

He had been wanted by authorities ever since, accused of embezzling public funds to hold an illegal independence referendum when he was head of Catalonia's regional government. 

Judge Pablo Llarena lifted the arrest warrant shortly after Spain's Constitutional Court ruled that a 2024 amnesty for Catalan separatists also applied to embezzlement cases.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the decision, saying it would allow Catalonia to "look to the future."

"We should celebrate that this also helps Catalan society, as it has been demanding throughout this time," he told journalists in Madrid.

How did the amnesty come about?

While Puigdemont and other members of his government fled abroad after the 2017 independence bid, several Catalan ministers who remained in Spain were sentenced to lengthy prison terms.

In 2024, in the face of strong opposition from Spain's conservative and right-wing parties, the Sanchez government passed an amnesty law. It intended to cover all offenses related to the secession attempt and ease tensions in the Catalonia region.

It also allowed Sanchez to secure the backing of Catalan separatist parties and stay in power after a 2023 election produced no clear majority.

But Puigdemont's Junts party withdrew its support last year, accusing Sanchez of failing to fulfill promises such as providing amnesty for its leader.

Around 400 separatists have benefited from the amnesty, but Puigdemont had been excluded because Spain's Supreme Court initially ruled the law did not apply to those accused of embezzlement. That changed after the Constitutional Court on Tuesday sided with one of Puigdemont's allies who had appealed against the top court's ruling.

Last week, Junts voted against housing relief measures proposed by Sanchez's government amid huge protests, prompting the prime minister on Monday to call a snap vote for November 29.
